question.prompt: Five different awards are to be given to three students. Each student will receive at least one award. In how many different ways can the awards be distributed?

solutions.explanation:
Since every student receives at least one award, the five awards can split only as \(2,2,1\) or \(3,1,1\). Count these two cases separately.

For the \(2,2,1\) pattern, choose the student receiving one award in \(3\) ways, then that student's award in \(5\) ways. Of the remaining four awards, choose two for one fixed remaining student; there are \(4\cdot3/2=6\) choices, since choosing the same pair in reverse order changes nothing. The other student receives the last two. This gives \(3\cdot5\cdot6=90\) distributions.

For the \(3,1,1\) pattern, choose the student receiving three awards in \(3\) ways. Choose those three awards in \(10\) ways, equivalently by choosing which two of five remain. Assign the two remaining awards to the two other students in \(2\) ways. This gives \(3\cdot10\cdot2=60\) distributions.

The total is \(90+60=\boxed{150}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\). Keeping the students distinct while treating each student's group of awards as unordered prevents extra factors from entering the count.
solutions.title: Split the positive award counts into two distribution patterns
